claim: Human ATG2A is 1938 residues long.
source: The 1938 residue-long ATG2A is folded into a 20 nm-long, 30 Å-wide rod with both tips composed of Pfam database-registered conserved domains: a 'Chorein_N' domain at the N-terminus of one tip (referred to as the N tip) and an 'ATG2_CAD' domain in the middle of the sequence of the other tip (referred to as the CAD tip) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the length of ATG2A as 1938 residues, referencing previous structural characterization work (Chowdhury et al., 2018).

claim: ATG2A is folded into a 20 nm-long, 30 Å-wide rod structure.
source: The 1938 residue-long ATG2A is folded into a 20 nm-long, 30 Å-wide rod with both tips composed of Pfam database-registered conserved domains: a 'Chorein_N' domain at the N-terminus of one tip (referred to as the N tip) and an 'ATG2_CAD' domain in the middle of the sequence of the other tip (referred to as the CAD tip) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The structural dimensions are stated based on previous structural characterization (Chowdhury et al., 2018).

claim: ATG2A contains a Chorein_N domain at the N-terminus.
source: The 1938 residue-long ATG2A is folded into a 20 nm-long, 30 Å-wide rod with both tips composed of Pfam database-registered conserved domains: a 'Chorein_N' domain at the N-terminus of one tip (referred to as the N tip) and an 'ATG2_CAD' domain in the middle of the sequence of the other tip (referred to as the CAD tip) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The presence of the Chorein_N domain is stated based on Pfam database registration and previous structural work.

claim: ATG2A contains an ATG2_CAD domain at the CAD tip.
source: The 1938 residue-long ATG2A is folded into a 20 nm-long, 30 Å-wide rod with both tips composed of Pfam database-registered conserved domains: a 'Chorein_N' domain at the N-terminus of one tip (referred to as the N tip) and an 'ATG2_CAD' domain in the middle of the sequence of the other tip (referred to as the CAD tip) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The presence of the ATG2_CAD domain is stated based on Pfam database registration and previous structural work.

claim: The Chorein_N domain is found at the N-terminus of VPS13 family proteins.
source: Chorein is one of vacuolar protein sorting 13 (VPS13) family proteins that function at contact sites between various organelles (Kumar et al., 2018; Lang et al., 2015; Murley and Nunnari, 2016; Park et al., 2016); as the name suggests, the Chorein_N domain is found at the N-terminus of VPS13 proteins (Pfisterer et al., 2014; Velayos-Baeza et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous literature about VPS13 proteins.

claim: VPS13 family proteins function at contact sites between various organelles.
source: Chorein is one of vacuolar protein sorting 13 (VPS13) family proteins that function at contact sites between various organelles (Kumar et al., 2018; Lang et al., 2015; Murley and Nunnari, 2016; Park et al., 2016); as the name suggests, the Chorein_N domain is found at the N-terminus of VPS13 proteins (Pfisterer et al., 2014; Velayos-Baeza et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated based on multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: WIPI4 is tightly bound adjacent to the CAD tip of ATG2A.
source: The ATG2_CAD domain is unique to ATG2, and WIPI4 is tightly bound adjacent to the CAD tip (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated based on previous structural characterization work (Chowdhury et al., 2018).

claim: The yeast Atg2-Atg18 and rat ATG2B-WIPI4 complexes exhibit similar overall shapes to human ATG2A-WIPI4.
source: The yeast Atg2-Atg18 and the rat ATG2B-WIPI4 complexes exhibit similar overall shapes, suggesting that the structure is evolutionarily conserved and, therefore, likely important for the function of these complexes (Chowdhury et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The structure of ATG2-WIPI complexes is evolutionarily conserved.
source: The yeast Atg2-Atg18 and the rat ATG2B-WIPI4 complexes exhibit similar overall shapes, suggesting that the structure is evolutionarily conserved and, therefore, likely important for the function of these complexes (Chowdhury et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar shapes across species.

claim: Each tip of the ATG2A rod can bind to a membrane.
source: Indeed, each tip of the ATG2A rod can bind to a membrane, and simultaneous membrane binding of both tips results in tethering the two membranes ~ 10–20 nm apart (Chowdhury et al., 2018), the typical distance observed at various organelle contact sites (Gatta and Levine, 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental work (Chowdhury et al., 2018).

claim: Simultaneous membrane binding of both tips of ATG2A results in tethering two membranes approximately 10-20 nm apart.
source: Indeed, each tip of the ATG2A rod can bind to a membrane, and simultaneous membrane binding of both tips results in tethering the two membranes ~ 10–20 nm apart (Chowdhury et al., 2018), the typical distance observed at various organelle contact sites (Gatta and Levine, 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental work (Chowdhury et al., 2018).

claim: The typical distance at organelle contact sites is 10-20 nm.
source: Indeed, each tip of the ATG2A rod can bind to a membrane, and simultaneous membrane binding of both tips results in tethering the two membranes ~ 10–20 nm apart (Chowdhury et al., 2018), the typical distance observed at various organelle contact sites (Gatta and Levine, 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous literature (Gatta and Levine, 2017).

claim: ATG2 proteins rely on lipid-packing defects in the membrane bilayer to effect membrane binding.
source: ATG2 proteins rely on lipid-packing defects in the membrane bilayer to effect membrane binding: Atg2 associates with giant unilamellar vesicles containing phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), a lipid molecule with a small head group that introduces packing defects (Gómez-Sánchez et al., 2018), as well as small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) (Kotani et al., 2018), whose high curvatures create lipid-packing defects (Harayama and Riezman, 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) is a lipid molecule with a small head group that introduces packing defects.
source: ATG2 proteins rely on lipid-packing defects in the membrane bilayer to effect membrane binding: Atg2 associates with giant unilamellar vesicles containing phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), a lipid molecule with a small head group that introduces packing defects (Gómez-Sánchez et al., 2018), as well as small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) (Kotani et al., 2018), whose high curvatures create lipid-packing defects (Harayama and Riezman, 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work (Gómez-Sánchez et al., 2018).

claim: Small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) have high curvatures that create lipid-packing defects.
source: ATG2 proteins rely on lipid-packing defects in the membrane bilayer to effect membrane binding: Atg2 associates with giant unilamellar vesicles containing phosphatidylethanolamine (PE), a lipid molecule with a small head group that introduces packing defects (Gómez-Sánchez et al., 2018), as well as small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) (Kotani et al., 2018), whose high curvatures create lipid-packing defects (Harayama and Riezman, 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous literature.

claim: ATG2A associates tightly with SUVs.
source: ATG2A also associates tightly with SUVs but only weakly with large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) (Chowdhury et al., 2018), whose lower curvatures create fewer lipid-packing defects.
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental work (Chowdhury et al., 2018).

claim: ATG2A associates only weakly with large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs).
source: ATG2A also associates tightly with SUVs but only weakly with large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) (Chowdhury et al., 2018), whose lower curvatures create fewer lipid-packing defects.
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental work (Chowdhury et al., 2018).

claim: Large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) have lower curvatures that create fewer lipid-packing defects.
source: ATG2A also associates tightly with SUVs but only weakly with large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) (Chowdhury et al., 2018), whose lower curvatures create fewer lipid-packing defects.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the weak interaction with LUVs.

claim: ATG2A/Atg2 tethers SUVs.
source: In correlation with the strength of the interactions, ATG2A/Atg2 tethers SUVs (Figure 1B) (Chowdhury et al., 2018; Kotani et al., 2018), while ATG2A cannot tether LUVs (Figure 1C) (Chowdhury et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental work and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ATG2A cannot tether LUVs.
source: In correlation with the strength of the interactions, ATG2A/Atg2 tethers SUVs (Figure 1B) (Chowdhury et al., 2018; Kotani et al., 2018), while ATG2A cannot tether LUVs (Figure 1C) (Chowdhury et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental work and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ATG2A-WIPI4 complex can mediate homotypic tethering between two PI3P-containing LUVs.
source: However, the ATG2A-WIPI4 complex can mediate homotypic tethering between two PI3P-containing LUVs as well as heterotypic tethering between a PI3P-containing LUV and a PI3P-free LUV (Figure 1D) (Chowdhury et al., 2018), presumably because the N tip has affinity to LUVs and WIPI4 can direct the CAD tip to the PI3P-containing LUV.
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental work and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The ATG2A-WIPI4 complex can mediate heterotypic tethering between a PI3P-containing LUV and a PI3P-free LUV.
source: However, the ATG2A-WIPI4 complex can mediate homotypic tethering between two PI3P-containing LUVs as well as heterotypic tethering between a PI3P-containing LUV and a PI3P-free LUV (Figure 1D) (Chowdhury et al., 2018), presumably because the N tip has affinity to LUVs and WIPI4 can direct the CAD tip to the PI3P-containing LUV.
evidence: This is stated based on previous experimental work and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The N tip of ATG2A has affinity to LUVs.
source: However, the ATG2A-WIPI4 complex can mediate homotypic tethering between two PI3P-containing LUVs as well as heterotypic tethering between a PI3P-containing LUV and a PI3P-free LUV (Figure 1D) (Chowdhury et al., 2018), presumably because the N tip has affinity to LUVs and WIPI4 can direct the CAD tip to the PI3P-containing LUV.
evidence: This is stated as a presumed explanation for the tethering activity.

claim: WIPI4 can direct the CAD tip of ATG2A to PI3P-containing LUVs.
source: However, the ATG2A-WIPI4 complex can mediate homotypic tethering between two PI3P-containing LUVs as well as heterotypic tethering between a PI3P-containing LUV and a PI3P-free LUV (Figure 1D) (Chowdhury et al., 2018), presumably because the N tip has affinity to LUVs and WIPI4 can direct the CAD tip to the PI3P-containing LUV.
evidence: This is stated as a presumed explanation for the tethering activity.

claim: The ATG2A-WIPI4 complex tethers PI3P-positive phagophores to neighboring membranes such as the ER and vesicles.
source: These data led us to propose that the ATG2A-WIPI4 complex tethers PI3P-positive phagophores to neighboring membranes, such as the ER and vesicles (Chowdhury et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal based on previous data.

claim: The Atg2-Atg18 complex mediates the ER-phagophore association in yeast.
source: This model is supported by yeast studies concluding that the Atg2-Atg18 complex mediates the ER-phagophore association (Gómez-Sánchez et al., 2018; Kotani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to yeast studies.

claim: ATG2A contains an ATG_C domain at the C-terminus.
source: ATG2 contains two additional conserved regions: an 'ATG_C' domain, also registered in Pfam and located at the end of the C-terminus; and another short region preceding the ATG_C domain (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ATG_C domains are found in VPS13 proteins.
source: Despite the name, ATG_C domains are also found in VPS13 proteins and are responsible for the localization of both ATG2A/B and VPS13 proteins to lipid droplets (Kumar et al., 2018; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous literature.

claim: ATG_C domains are responsible for the localization of ATG2A/B and VPS13 proteins to lipid droplets.
source: Despite the name, ATG_C domains are also found in VPS13 proteins and are responsible for the localization of both ATG2A/B and VPS13 proteins to lipid droplets (Kumar et al., 2018; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous literature.

claim: The ATG_C domain of ATG2A/B is dispensable for autophagy.
source: Consistently, the ATG_C domain of ATG2A/B is dispensable for autophagy (Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The C-terminal localization region (CLR) is required for the localization of ATG2A/B and Atg2 to phagophores.
source: In contrast, the region preceding the ATG_C domain is required for the localization of ATG2A/B and Atg2 to phagophores (Kotani et al., 2018; Tamura et al., 2017; Velikkakath et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous literature.

claim: The CLR contains amphipathic α-helices that can associate with membranes.
source: This region, referred to as the C-terminal localization region (CLR), contains amphipathic α-helices that can associate with membranes (Chowdhury et al., 2018; Kotani et al., 2018; Tamura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous literature.

claim: The CLR of yeast Atg2 is required for the membrane tethering activity of this protein in vitro.
source: The CLR of yeast Atg2 is required for the membrane tethering activity of this protein in vitro (Kotani et al., 2018) but is not required for that of ATG2A, consistent with the structural observation that the rod is the membrane tethering unit of ATG2A (Chowdhury et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The CLR is not required for the membrane tethering activity of ATG2A.
source: The CLR of yeast Atg2 is required for the membrane tethering activity of this protein in vitro (Kotani et al., 2018) but is not required for that of ATG2A, consistent with the structural observation that the rod is the membrane tethering unit of ATG2A (Chowdhury et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The rod is the membrane tethering unit of ATG2A.
source: The CLR of yeast Atg2 is required for the membrane tethering activity of this protein in vitro (Kotani et al., 2018) but is not required for that of ATG2A, consistent with the structural observation that the rod is the membrane tethering unit of ATG2A (Chowdhury et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous structural work.

claim: The C-terminus of ATG2A/B is flexible.
source: Previous structural studies could not identify the location of the ATG2A/B C-terminus in the electron microscopy (EM) maps, suggesting that the C-terminus is flexible (Chowdhury et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to identify the C-terminus in EM maps in previous studies.

claim: The flexibility of the C-terminal regions may be advantageous for their function as localization determinants.
source: Such flexibility may be advantageous for the C-terminal regions to function sufficiently as localization determinants (Kotani et al., 2018; Tamura et al., 2017; Velikkakath et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on citations to previous work.

claim: VPS13 family proteins are lipid transfer proteins.
source: This hypothesis is strongly supported by a recent study reporting that VPS13 family proteins are lipid transfer proteins (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to a recent study.

claim: The crystal structure of the N-terminal 335-residue-long fragment of Chaetomium thermophilum Vps13p revealed a unique structure with a large hydrophobic cavity.
source: The crystal structure of the N-terminal 335-residue-long fragment of Chaetomium thermophilum Vps13p revealed a unique structure with a large hydrophobic cavity that was suggested to accommodate lipid molecules.
evidence: This is stated based on the crystal structure reported by Kumar et al., 2018.

claim: The hydrophobic cavity in Vps13p was suggested to accommodate lipid molecules.
source: The crystal structure of the N-terminal 335-residue-long fragment of Chaetomium thermophilum Vps13p revealed a unique structure with a large hydrophobic cavity that was suggested to accommodate lipid molecules.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion from the structural study.

claim: An N-terminal 1350-residue-long construct of S. cerevisiae Vps13p (Vps13α) can bind approximately 10 glycerolipid molecules with broad specificity.
source: An N-terminal 1350-residue-long construct of S. cerevisiae Vps13p termed Vps13α was shown to bind an unusually large number (~10) of glycerolipid molecules with a broad specificity and transfer those lipids between membranes.
evidence: This is stated based on the study by Kumar et al., 2018.

claim: Vps13α transfers lipids between membranes.
source: An N-terminal 1350-residue-long construct of S. cerevisiae Vps13p termed Vps13α was shown to bind an unusually large number (~10) of glycerolipid molecules with a broad specificity and transfer those lipids between membranes.
evidence: This is stated based on the study by Kumar et al., 2018.

claim: Homology modeling suggests that the structure of the ATG2 N-terminus would be very similar to that of Vps13p.
source: Homology modeling suggests that the structure of the ATG2 N-terminus would be very similar to that of Vps13p (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated based on homology modeling and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The VPS13 structure and the ATG2A structure proposed by homology modeling fit into the N tip of the negative stain EM density map of ATG2A and occupy approximately 20-25% of the total volume.
source: The VPS13 structure and the ATG2A structure proposed by the homology model fit into the N tip of our previous negative stain EM density map of ATG2A and occupy ~20–25% of the total volume (Figure 1A) (Otomo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on fitting the homology model into the EM map.

claim: The central β-sheet of the ATG2A N-terminus is expected to extend in the C-terminal direction in the full-length protein.
source: The central β-sheet, which serves as the base of this structure, is expected to extend in the C-terminal direction in the full-length protein (Kumar et al., 2018), which would create an elongated groove-shaped hydrophobic cavity in the ATG2A rod.
evidence: This is stated as an expectation based on the VPS13 structure.

claim: An elongated groove-shaped hydrophobic cavity in the ATG2A rod could accommodate a large number of lipids.
source: The central β-sheet, which serves as the base of this structure, is expected to extend in the C-terminal direction in the full-length protein (Kumar et al., 2018), which would create an elongated groove-shaped hydrophobic cavity in the ATG2A rod. Such a cavity could accommodate a large number of lipids, as previously reported for VPS13 (Kumar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the VPS13 structure.

claim: Cryo-EM 2D class averages of the ATG2A-WIPI4 complex indicated that the specimen was not of sufficient quality for high-resolution structure determination.
source: These 2D images indicated that the specimen was not of sufficient quality for high-resolution structure determination but could visualize the predicted internal cavity of ATG2A, which appears to extend from the N tip to the CAD tip, supporting the hypothesis that ATG2A may be a lipid-binding/transfer protein.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryo-EM analysis performed in this study.

claim: Cryo-EM 2D class averages of the ATG2A-WIPI4 complex visualized the predicted internal cavity of ATG2A.
source: These 2D images indicated that the specimen was not of sufficient quality for high-resolution structure determination but could visualize the predicted internal cavity of ATG2A, which appears to extend from the N tip to the CAD tip, supporting the hypothesis that ATG2A may be a lipid-binding/transfer protein.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryo-EM analysis performed in this study.

claim: The internal cavity of ATG2A appears to extend from the N tip to the CAD tip.
source: These 2D images indicated that the specimen was not of sufficient quality for high-resolution structure determination but could visualize the predicted internal cavity of ATG2A, which appears to extend from the N tip to the CAD tip, supporting the hypothesis that ATG2A may be a lipid-binding/transfer protein.
evidence: This is stated based on the cryo-EM analysis performed in this study.

claim: ATG2A can extract NBD-PE from membranes.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that ATG2A can extract NBD-PE from membranes and dissociate from the membrane with those lipids attached.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid extraction assay results shown in Figure 2.

claim: ATG2A can dissociate from membranes with extracted lipids attached.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that ATG2A can extract NBD-PE from membranes and dissociate from the membrane with those lipids attached.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid extraction assay results shown in Figure 2.

claim: ATG2A unloads NBD-PE onto LUVs during a transient interaction with the LUVs.
source: These data indicate that ATG2A unloads NBD-PE onto LUVs during a transient interaction with the LUVs.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid unloading assay results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The lipid extraction and unloading capabilities of ATG2A define ATG2A as a lipid transfer protein.
source: In conclusion, the lipid extraction and unloading capabilities of ATG2A demonstrated here define ATG2A as a lipid transfer protein.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the extraction and unloading assay results.

claim: ATG2A facilitates lipid transfer between SUVs in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: ATG2A facilitated lipid transfer in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3C), suggesting that the reaction was catalyzed by ATG2A.
evidence: This is stated based on the titration experiment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The lipid transfer reaction is catalyzed by ATG2A.
source: ATG2A facilitated lipid transfer in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3C), suggesting that the reaction was catalyzed by ATG2A.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the concentration-dependent manner of lipid transfer.

claim: The fastest rate of NBD-PE transfer by ATG2A was approximately 0.017 s−1 per protein molecule.
source: The fastest rate of NBD-PE transfer was ~0.017 s−1 per protein molecule, which was observed at the two lowest protein concentrations (6 and 12 nM).
evidence: This is stated based on the titration experiment shown in Figure 3.

claim: The NBD-PE transfer rate of ATG2A is comparable to that of the Mmm1-Mdm12 complex.
source: This transfer rate is comparable to the NBD-PE transfer rate of the Mmm1-Mdm12 complex, the lipid transfer machinery that exchanges PE and PS between ER and mitochondria (Kawano et al., 2018), but it is much slower than the rate of cholesterol transfer by OSBP between ER and Golgi (~1 s−1 per protein molecule)(Mesmin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with published rates from other lipid transfer proteins.

claim: The NBD-PE transfer rate of ATG2A is much slower than the rate of cholesterol transfer by OSBP.
source: This transfer rate is comparable to the NBD-PE transfer rate of the Mmm1-Mdm12 complex, the lipid transfer machinery that exchanges PE and PS between ER and mitochondria (Kawano et al., 2018), but it is much slower than the rate of cholesterol transfer by OSBP between ER and Golgi (~1 s−1 per protein molecule)(Mesmin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with published rates from other lipid transfer proteins.

claim: Lipid transfer between 25% POPS-containing PO SUVs was slower than that between 25% DOPS-containing DO SUVs.
source: Lipid transfer between 25% POPS-containing PO SUVs was slower than that between 25% DOPS-containing DO SUVs (Figure 3C and E), and the more POPS the SUV contained, the faster the lipid transfer was.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figures 3C and 3E.

claim: The more POPS the SUV contained, the faster the lipid transfer was.
source: Lipid transfer between 25% POPS-containing PO SUVs was slower than that between 25% DOPS-containing DO SUVs (Figure 3C and E), and the more POPS the SUV contained, the faster the lipid transfer was.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There was approximately a twofold difference in the transfer rate between 25% and 0% POPS SUVs.
source: There was approximately a twofold difference in the transfer rate between 25% and 0% POPS (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: All PO SUVs with varying POPS percentages clustered in the presence of ATG2A.
source: We performed DLS experiments to examine tethering of these PO SUVs and confirmed that all SUVs clustered in the presence of ATG2A (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated based on DLS experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: POPS facilitates both membrane tethering and lipid transfer by ATG2A.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that POPS facilitates both membrane tethering and lipid transfer.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the DLS and lipid transfer assay results.

claim: The effect of POPS on lipid transfer appears to be based on its negative charge.
source: The effect of POPS appears to be based on its negative charge because the replacement of POPS with another negatively charged lipid, phosphatidylinositol (PI), yielded a similar trend in the lipid transfer assay (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ATG2A can mediate lipid transfer between membranes with near-physiological lipid compositions.
source: While this finding could suggest that ATG2A may not be operating at its full capacity in cells, these experiments with PO lipids demonstrated that ATG2A can mediate lipid transfer between membranes with near-physiological lipid compositions.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results with PO lipids.

claim: ATG2A12×D exhibited lipid transfer activity between DO SUVs, but its transfer rate was only approximately 1/3 of that of the wild-type protein.
source: As shown in Figure 3G, ATG2A12×D exhibited lipid transfer activity between DO SUVs, but its transfer rate was only ~1/3 of that of the wild-type protein (Figure 3D and H).
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figures 3G and 3H.

claim: The lipid transfer between PO SUVs by ATG2A12×D was only slightly slower compared with the wild-type protein.
source: However, the lipid transfer between PO SUVs was only slightly slower compared with the same experiment with the wild-type protein (Figures 3E, F, I and J).
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figures 3E, F, I, and J.

claim: The CLR and non-physiological DO lipids including high percentage of DOPS synergized in promoting tethering and lipid transfer by the wild-type protein.
source: Thus, it appears that the CLR and non-physiological DO lipids including the high percentage of DOPS synergized in promoting tethering and lipid transfer by the wild-type protein, but in more physiological PO lipids-based conditions, the CLR contributes much less to lipid transfer and perhaps to membrane tethering as well.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results comparing wild-type and mutant ATG2A.

claim: In more physiological PO lipids-based conditions, the CLR contributes much less to lipid transfer and perhaps to membrane tethering.
source: Thus, it appears that the CLR and non-physiological DO lipids including the high percentage of DOPS synergized in promoting tethering and lipid transfer by the wild-type protein, but in more physiological PO lipids-based conditions, the CLR contributes much less to lipid transfer and perhaps to membrane tethering as well.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results comparing wild-type and mutant ATG2A.

claim: The rod region of the ATG2A protein is the core catalytic domain for both membrane tethering and lipid transfer.
source: Together with our previous data indicating that the rod-shaped part of ATG2A tethers membranes and the CLR is dispensable for membrane tethering (Chowdhury et al., 2018), the presented results confirm that the rod region of the ATG2A protein is the core catalytic domain for both membrane tethering and lipid transfer.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the current and previous data.

claim: ATG2A alone slightly increased NBD fluorescence in the lipid transfer assay with PI3P-containing donor LUVs and PI3P-free acceptor LUVs.
source: In the absence of WIPI4, ATG2A (100 nM) slightly increased NBD fluorescence (Figure 4B), suggesting that ATG2A can transfer lipids between nontethered donors and acceptors but does so inefficiently.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ATG2A can transfer lipids between nontethered donors and acceptors but does so inefficiently.
source: In the absence of WIPI4, ATG2A (100 nM) slightly increased NBD fluorescence (Figure 4B), suggesting that ATG2A can transfer lipids between nontethered donors and acceptors but does so inefficiently.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The addition of WIPI4 to ATG2A resulted in the acceleration of lipid transfer in a WIPI4 concentration-dependent manner.
source: Strikingly, the addition of WIPI4 to ATG2A resulted in the acceleration of lipid transfer in a WIPI4 concentration-dependent manner, whereas the signal was not altered with WIPI4 alone (100 nM), demonstrating that WIPI4 facilitates ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: WIPI4 alone did not alter the lipid transfer signal.
source: Strikingly, the addition of WIPI4 to ATG2A resulted in the acceleration of lipid transfer in a WIPI4 concentration-dependent manner, whereas the signal was not altered with WIPI4 alone (100 nM), demonstrating that WIPI4 facilitates ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: WIPI4 facilitates ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer.
source: Strikingly, the addition of WIPI4 to ATG2A resulted in the acceleration of lipid transfer in a WIPI4 concentration-dependent manner, whereas the signal was not altered with WIPI4 alone (100 nM), demonstrating that WIPI4 facilitates ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstration based on the lipid transfer assay results.

claim: The lipid transfer rate increased linearly with the concentration of WIPI4 and nearly saturated at the 1:1 stoichiometric concentration of WIPI4 to ATG2A.
source: Notably, the lipid transfer rate increased linearly with the concentration of WIPI4 and nearly saturated at the 1:1 stoichiometric concentration of WIPI4 to ATG2A (Figure 4C), consistent with the strong interaction between WIPI4 and ATG2A.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Lipid transfer is facilitated by ATG2A-mediated membrane tethering.
source: Based on these data, the above finding that ATG2A alone can transfer lipids between tethered SUVs, and the observation that the ATG2A-WIPI4 complex tethers PI3P-containing LUVs to PI3P-free LUVs (Chowdhury et al., 2018), we concluded that lipid transfer is facilitated by ATG2A-mediated membrane tethering.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the current and previous data.

claim: ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer is a bidirectional reaction.
source: Thus, ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer is a bidirectional reaction, and it is therefore likely that in both experiments, non-fluorescent lipids are also being transferred in both directions.
evidence: This is stated based on the comparison of lipid transfer assays with reversed orientations of PI3P-containing and PI3P-free LUVs.

claim: Membrane tethering is required for ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer between membranes with physiological lipid compositions.
source: Taken together, we conclude that membrane tethering is required for ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer between membranes with physiological lipid compositions, and lipid-packing defects of substrate membranes are crucial for lipid transfer.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the lipid transfer assay results with various lipid compositions.

claim: Lipid-packing defects of substrate membranes are crucial for lipid transfer by ATG2A.
source: Taken together, we conclude that membrane tethering is required for ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer between membranes with physiological lipid compositions, and lipid-packing defects of substrate membranes are crucial for lipid transfer.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the lipid transfer assay results with various lipid compositions.

claim: WIPI1 can facilitate ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer.
source: Thus, WIPI1 can facilitate ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer, but it can do so only at a concentration below that of ATG2A.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results with WIPI1 shown in Figure 4J-L.

claim: WIPI1 can facilitate ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer only at a concentration below that of ATG2A.
source: Thus, WIPI1 can facilitate ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer, but it can do so only at a concentration below that of ATG2A.
evidence: This is stated based on the lipid transfer assay results with WIPI1 shown in Figure 4J-L.

claim: WIPI1 clusters PI3P-containing LUVs.
source: To investigate this possibility, we performed turbidity assays with PI3P-containing LUVs and WIPI proteins and observed that the turbidity increased in a WIPI1 concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and B), indicating vesicle clustering by WIPI1.
evidence: This is stated based on the turbidity assay results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: WIPI4 does not cluster PI3P-containing LUVs.
source: The liposome clustering was limited to WIPI1 because, in the presence of WIPI4, the turbidity did not increase (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A and B), and the liposomes were spread out in the EM images (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is stated based on the turbidity assay and EM results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: WIPI1-induced aggregation of PI3P-containing donor LUVs results in the sequestration of the proteins and donor LUVs from the PI3P-free acceptor LUVs, leading to the suppression of ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer at higher concentrations of WIPI1.
source: Thus, WIPI1-induced aggregation of PI3P-containing donor LUVs would result in the sequestration of the proteins and donor LUVs from the PI3P-free acceptor LUVs, leading to the suppression of ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer at higher concentrations of WIPI1.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the suppression of lipid transfer at high WIPI1 concentrations.

claim: Free WIPI1 does not bind to bead-immobilized ATG2A in an affinity pull-down assay.
source: We first tested the bimolecular interaction between WIPI1 and ATG2A using an affinity pull-down assay, which detected no binding of free WIPI1 to bead-immobilized ATG2A (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated based on the affinity pull-down assay results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WIPI4 stably associates with ATG2A in an affinity pull-down assay.
source: The same assay with WIPI4 showed its stable association with ATG2A, contrasting to the result with WIPI1.
evidence: This is stated based on the affinity pull-down assay results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: WIPI4 and ATG2A cooperatively associate with PI3P-containing membranes.
source: In stark contrast, in the presence of WIPI4, ATG2A was recovered almost completely from the top fractions (Figure 5C; lanes 7–12), and WIPI4 recovery from the top fraction (~100% at 100 nM) was improved greatly compared to that in the WIPI4-only experiments (~20% at 100 nM) (Figure 5B, lanes 4–9), indicating that WIPI4 and ATG2A cooperatively associate with PI3P-containing membranes.
evidence: This is stated based on the liposome flotation assay results shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: WIPI1 promotes membrane recruitment of ATG2A to PI3P-containing membranes.
source: The experiments with WIPI1 yielded similar results (Figure 5C; lanes 13–18), demonstrating ATG2A recruitment to PI3P-containing membranes in the presence of WIPI1.
evidence: This is stated based on the liposome flotation assay results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the presence of either WIPI protein, ATG2A binds stably to PI3P-containing membranes.
source: In conclusion, in the presence of either WIPI protein, ATG2A binds stably to PI3P-containing membranes, providing the basis for WIPI-enabled membrane tethering and lipid transfer as demonstrated above.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the liposome flotation assay results.

claim: The Atg2-Atg18 complex directly tethers the phagophore to the ER in yeast.
source: Recent yeast studies suggested that the Atg2-Atg18 complex directly tethers the phagophore to the ER (Gómez-Sánchez et al., 2018; Kotani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to recent yeast studies.

claim: Atg18 is on the edge of PI3P-positive phagophores.
source: Atg18 is on the edge of PI3P-positive phagophores (Graef et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013), directing the CAD tip of Atg2 to the phagophore and the N tip to the ER (Graef, 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Atg18 directs the CAD tip of Atg2 to the phagophore and the N tip to the ER.
source: Atg18 is on the edge of PI3P-positive phagophores (Graef et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013), directing the CAD tip of Atg2 to the phagophore and the N tip to the ER (Graef, 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The N-terminal 21 residues of yeast Atg2 are required for ER anchoring.
source: ER anchoring by the N tip was demonstrated by Kotani et al., who created an autophagy-deficient Atg2 mutant by deleting the N-terminal 21 residues and restored autophagic activity by genetically fusing the transmembrane domain of the ER resident Sec71 protein to the N-terminus of the mutant (Kotani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to the work by Kotani et al., 2018.

claim: ATG2A is localized to the ER-phagophore contact site together with WIPI2.
source: In mammals, the precise location of ATG2A/B on the expanding phagophore had not been established until very recently, but during the revision of this manuscript, Valverde et al. reported that ATG2A is localized to the ER-phagophore contact site together with WIPI2 (Valverde et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to the work by Valverde et al., 2019.

claim: The edge of the phagophore forms a PI3P-enriched transient region called the 'omegasome'.
source: The edge of the phagophore has been suggested to form a PI3P-enriched transient region called the 'omegasome' (Axe et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: WIPI4 localizes to the omegasome.
source: The mechanism by which ATG2A localizes to the omegasome is not known but likely involves its interaction with WIPI proteins including WIPI4, which has been shown to localize to the omegasome (Lu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: Direct tethering of the ER and the phagophore edge by the ATG2-WIPI complex would allow the transfer of ER lipids to the phagophore, driving phagophore expansion.
source: Direct tethering of the ER and the phagophore edge by the ATG2-WIPI complex would allow the transfer of ER lipids to the phagophore, driving phagophore expansion (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated as a model based on the current findings and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The model of phagophore expansion based on non-vesicular lipid transfer explains why the edge of the phagophore remains associated with the ER during its expansion.
source: This model of phagophore expansion based on non-vesicular lipid transfer explains why and how the edge of the phagophore remains associated with the ER during its expansion (Graef et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013) and why autophagosome membranes are of thinner types like the ER membrane (Arstila and Trump, 1968) but are devoid of ER membrane-bound proteins/markers such as cytochrome P-450, Dpm1, and GFP-HDEL (Suzuki et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as an explanation based on the proposed model and citations to previous observations.

claim: Autophagosome membranes are of thinner types like the ER membrane.
source: This model of phagophore expansion based on non-vesicular lipid transfer explains why and how the edge of the phagophore remains associated with the ER during its expansion (Graef et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013) and why autophagosome membranes are of thinner types like the ER membrane (Arstila and Trump, 1968) but are devoid of ER membrane-bound proteins/markers such as cytochrome P-450, Dpm1, and GFP-HDEL (Suzuki et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: Autophagosome membranes are devoid of ER membrane-bound proteins/markers such as cytochrome P-450, Dpm1, and GFP-HDEL.
source: This model of phagophore expansion based on non-vesicular lipid transfer explains why and how the edge of the phagophore remains associated with the ER during its expansion (Graef et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013) and why autophagosome membranes are of thinner types like the ER membrane (Arstila and Trump, 1968) but are devoid of ER membrane-bound proteins/markers such as cytochrome P-450, Dpm1, and GFP-HDEL (Suzuki et al., 2013; Yamamoto et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous work.

claim: The ER-staining lipophilic dye octadecyl rhodamine B also stains the phagophore in yeast.
source: Moreover, the recent observation that the ER-staining lipophilic dye octadecyl rhodamine B also stains the phagophore in yeast (Hirata et al., 2017) can be explained by the ATG2-mediated transfer of this lipophilic dye from the ER to the phagophore.
evidence: This is stated based on citation to a recent observation.

claim: The observation that octadecyl rhodamine B stains the phagophore can be explained by ATG2-mediated transfer of this lipophilic dye from the ER to the phagophore.
source: Moreover, the recent observation that the ER-staining lipophilic dye octadecyl rhodamine B also stains the phagophore in yeast (Hirata et al., 2017) can be explained by the ATG2-mediated transfer of this lipophilic dye from the ER to the phagophore.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation based on the proposed model.

claim: The phagophore edge is likely abundant in lipid packing defects created by its high curvature with a diameter of approximately 30 nm.
source: On the one hand, the phagophore edge is likely abundant in both of these factors: the lipid packing defects created by its high curvature with a diameter of ~30 nm (Nguyen et al., 2017) and the negative charges resulting from the local production of PI3P.
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work and inference about the phagophore edge properties.

claim: The phagophore edge has negative charges resulting from the local production of PI3P.
source: On the one hand, the phagophore edge is likely abundant in both of these factors: the lipid packing defects created by its high curvature with a diameter of ~30 nm (Nguyen et al., 2017) and the negative charges resulting from the local production of PI3P.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the phagophore edge properties.

claim: In yeast, the phagophore edge is located at the ER exit site (ERES).
source: In yeast, the phagophore edge has been shown to be located at the ER exit site (ERES) (Graef et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013), the place where COPII vesicles are generated.
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous yeast studies.

claim: The ERES is the place where COPII vesicles are generated.
source: In yeast, the phagophore edge has been shown to be located at the ER exit site (ERES) (Graef et al., 2013; Suzuki et al., 2013), the place where COPII vesicles are generated.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: In mammals, the ERGIC and the ER-mitochondria contact site are adjacent to the phagophore.
source: In mammals, in addition to the ERES, it has also been suggested that the ERGIC and the ER-mitochondria contact site are adjacent to the phagophore (Ge et al., 2013; Ge et al., 2017; Hamasaki et al., 2013; Hayashi-Nishino et al., 2009; Karanasios et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous mammalian studies.

claim: PI has been shown to be enriched in the phagophore-contacting ER subdomain.
source: In terms of the negative charges of those membranes, PI has been shown to be enriched in the phagophore-contacting ER subdomain (Nishimura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: PI synthase localizes to the phagophore-contacting ER subdomain and generates PI molecules.
source: PI synthase localizes to this ER subdomain and generates PI molecules, which could be transferred to the phagophore by ATG2 to serve as the precursor of PI3P.
evidence: This is stated based on inference from the localization of PI synthase.

claim: PI molecules could be transferred to the phagophore by ATG2 to serve as the precursor of PI3P.
source: PI synthase localizes to this ER subdomain and generates PI molecules, which could be transferred to the phagophore by ATG2 to serve as the precursor of PI3P.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about the role of ATG2 in PI transfer.

claim: The rate of lipid transfer by individual ATG2A molecules seems to be too slow to accomplish the task of creating an autophagosome.
source: However, the rate of lipid transfer by individual ATG2A molecules estimated above seems to be too slow to accomplish this enormous task and therefore must be accelerated much more.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the estimated lipid transfer rate.

claim: Unidirectional lipid transport must consume energy.
source: In a thermodynamic point of view, unidirectional lipid transport must consume energy, and by consuming energy, lipid transport could be greatly accelerated.
evidence: This is stated based on thermodynamic principles.

claim: Some yet-unidentified proteins are responsible for the energy-expending task of unidirectional lipid transport.
source: We speculate that some yet-unidentified proteins are responsible for this energy-expending task.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation.

claim: The number of PI3P molecules on the phagophore would determine the number of ATG2 proteins, thereby regulating the overall rate of phagophore growth.
source: The demonstration that WIPI proteins can facilitate ATG2A-mediated lipid transfer suggests that PI3P dynamics control phagophore expansion: the number of PI3P molecules on the phagophore would determine the number of ATG2 proteins, thereby regulating the overall rate of phagophore growth.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the current findings.

claim: A reduction in the PI3P level would release ATG2 from the point of ER-phagophore contact, leading to the disruption of the contact and the cessation of phagophore expansion.
source: A reduction in the PI3P level, which occurs toward the end of autophagosome formation (Axe et al., 2008), would release ATG2 from the point of ER-phagophore contact, leading to the disruption of the contact and the cessation of phagophore expansion.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the proposed model and citation to previous work.

claim: The overexpression of the PI3P-phosphatase myotubularin-related phosphatase three generates significantly smaller autophagosomes.
source: This model of the regulation of phagophore expansion is supported by the previous observation that the overexpression of the PI3P-phosphatase myotubularin-related phosphatase three generates significantly smaller autophagosomes (Taguchi-Atarashi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to a previous observation.

claim: The direct link between WIPIs and ATG2A/B has been limited to WIPI4.
source: In contrast, the direct link between WIPIs and ATG2A/B has been limited to WIPI4.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous knowledge.

claim: WIPI1 does not interact strongly with ATG2A/B.
source: Notably, our work now adds WIPI1 to this link, raising the possibility that the yet-untested WIPI2 and WIPI3, which, like WIPI1, do not interact strongly with ATG2A/B (Bakula et al., 2017), might also facilitate ATG2A recruitment.
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: WIPI2 and WIPI3 do not interact strongly with ATG2A/B.
source: Notably, our work now adds WIPI1 to this link, raising the possibility that the yet-untested WIPI2 and WIPI3, which, like WIPI1, do not interact strongly with ATG2A/B (Bakula et al., 2017), might also facilitate ATG2A recruitment.
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: WIPI2 and WIPI3 might also facilitate ATG2A recruitment.
source: Notably, our work now adds WIPI1 to this link, raising the possibility that the yet-untested WIPI2 and WIPI3, which, like WIPI1, do not interact strongly with ATG2A/B (Bakula et al., 2017), might also facilitate ATG2A recruitment.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the current findings with WIPI1.

claim: WIPI1 and WIPI2 have high sequence identity (approximately 80%).
source: The high sequence identity (~80%) between WIPI1 and WIPI2 (Polson et al., 2010) supports this potential role of WIPI2.
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The self-oligomerization of Atg18 on giant unilamellar vesicles tubulates the membranes.
source: It is noteworthy that the self-oligomerization of Atg18 on giant unilamellar vesicles tubulates the membranes (Scacioc et al., 2017), as such membrane tubulation activity may lead to the formation of the omegasome, which has been visualized by EM as a PI3P-positive thin tubular membrane at the phagophore edge (Uemura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The omegasome has been visualized by EM as a PI3P-positive thin tubular membrane at the phagophore edge.
source: It is noteworthy that the self-oligomerization of Atg18 on giant unilamellar vesicles tubulates the membranes (Scacioc et al., 2017), as such membrane tubulation activity may lead to the formation of the omegasome, which has been visualized by EM as a PI3P-positive thin tubular membrane at the phagophore edge (Uemura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: Membrane tubulation activity of WIPI proteins may lead to the formation of the omegasome.
source: It is noteworthy that the self-oligomerization of Atg18 on giant unilamellar vesicles tubulates the membranes (Scacioc et al., 2017), as such membrane tubulation activity may lead to the formation of the omegasome, which has been visualized by EM as a PI3P-positive thin tubular membrane at the phagophore edge (Uemura et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the membrane tubulation activity of Atg18.

claim: Yeast Atg2 transfers lipids between SUVs but poorly between LUVs.
source: A similar model has been proposed by Osawa et al., during our revision, who demonstrated that yeast Atg2 transfers lipids between SUVs but poorly between LUVs (Osawa et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to work by Osawa et al., 2019.

claim: A short (345 residues) ATG2A N-terminal fragment can mediate lipid transfer in vitro.
source: However, Valverde et al., who also reported the lipid transfer capacity of ATG2A, demonstrated that a short (345 residues) ATG2A N-terminal fragment can not only mediate lipid transfer in vitro but also rescue autophagy in ATG2A/B double knockout cells (under overexpressed conditions) (Valverde et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to work by Valverde et al., 2019.

claim: A short (345 residues) ATG2A N-terminal fragment can rescue autophagy in ATG2A/B double knockout cells under overexpressed conditions.
source: However, Valverde et al., who also reported the lipid transfer capacity of ATG2A, demonstrated that a short (345 residues) ATG2A N-terminal fragment can not only mediate lipid transfer in vitro but also rescue autophagy in ATG2A/B double knockout cells (under overexpressed conditions) (Valverde et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to work by Valverde et al., 2019.

claim: Osawa et al. succeeded in visualizing a lipid molecule (PE) in the hydrophobic cavity of the Atg2 N-terminus by X-ray crystallography.
source: On the structural side, Osawa et al. succeeded in visualizing a lipid molecule (PE) in the hydrophobic cavity of the Atg2 N-terminus by X-ray crystallography, providing a structural basis of lipid binding of the N-terminus.
evidence: This is stated based on the work by Osawa et al., 2019.
